edges.mechanism: Green tea/EGCG competitively inhibits intestinal OATP1A2 uptake of nadolol; nadolol AUC fell about 85% with 700 mL/day tea and its BP effect was blunted; a single cup cut AUC to 0.37 and the effect persisted 1 h later.
edges.evidence: Human crossover PK studies (n=10-13), case report of therapeutic failure, reviews; moderate certainty

edges.mechanism: Green tea extract (~300 mg EGCG) impaired intestinal absorption of lisinopril: AUC ratio 0.34, Cmax ratio 0.29; renal clearance unchanged.
edges.evidence: Single human crossover PK study (n=10); no outcome data; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Green tea extract 300-600 mg lowered atorvastatin AUC 22-24% and Cmax 24-25%; OATP1B1/1B3 uptake inhibition in vitro.
edges.evidence: Human crossover PK (n=12) plus in vitro transporter data; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Extract with 800 mg EGCG/day for 14 days lowered rosuvastatin AUC about 20%; single 300 mg EGCG lowered AUC 19% but effect disappeared after 10-day pretreatment.
edges.evidence: Two human PK studies with partly conflicting results; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Green tea is a vitamin K source; heavy intake (0.5-1 gallon/day) lowered INR from 3.79 to 1.14 with recovery after stopping. Listed among foods/herbs interacting with warfarin.
edges.evidence: Case report and systematic review; low certainty (applies mainly to large tea volumes)

edges.mechanism: EGCG and other 1,2-benzenediol polyphenols bind boronic-acid proteasome inhibitors and abolish bortezomib antitumor activity; in mice antagonism required EGCG plasma levels above 200 uM.
edges.evidence: Preclinical in vitro and xenograft data; no human outcome data; low certainty

edges.mechanism: EGCG inhibits OATP1A2-mediated uptake; green tea extract lowered fexofenadine AUC by 70%.
edges.evidence: Human crossover PK study (n=10); low certainty

edges.mechanism: Green tea lowered raloxifene AUC to about 0.60 of baseline after acute and chronic intake, likely via intestinal transporter inhibition.
edges.evidence: Human PK study (n=16); low certainty

edges.mechanism: Heavy home-made green tea intake was associated with a supratherapeutic tacrolimus trough (18.3 ng/mL) that normalized after stopping.
edges.evidence: Single case report; very low certainty

edges.mechanism: Green tea and EGCG inhibit OCT1, OCT2, MATE1 and MATE2-K transport of metformin in vitro; human relevance unknown.
edges.evidence: In vitro only; very low certainty

edges.mechanism: Caffeine in many extracts (often undeclared) adds sympathetic and BP effects to amphetamine; combined stimulant effects are poorly characterized.
edges.evidence: Product analysis and review of caffeine stimulant cardiovascular effects; very low certainty

edges.mechanism: Extracts contain variable caffeine (28-183 mg per unit in one survey); additive intake against the 400 mg/day adult reference; caffeine also raises EGCG exposure.
edges.evidence: Product analysis, human PK study, systematic review; moderate certainty

edges.mechanism: Theanine plus caffeine (both tea constituents) produced small acute improvements in attention and mood vs placebo.
edges.evidence: Systematic review and MA of RCTs; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Tea has little appreciable effect on heme-iron absorption in vivo, but EGCG and green tea extract inhibit heme-iron transfer dose-dependently in Caco-2 cells; separating doses is prudent.
edges.evidence: Clinical case report/review and in vitro data; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Tea polyphenols chelate non-heme iron; tea with a meal cut iron absorption by 37%, halved by a 1-h gap; tea blocked response to oral ferrous salts.
edges.evidence: Stable-isotope controlled trial, case reports, review; moderate certainty

edges.mechanism: Green tea extract lowered folic acid AUC 27-40% and catechins inhibit folate uptake and DHFR in vitro; 720-800 mg EGCG/day did not lower serum folate in 30 days. No data for 5-MTHF specifically.
edges.evidence: Human PK with folic acid, in vitro data, small clinical safety study; very low certainty for 5-MTHF

edges.mechanism: Both are among the 6 most frequently reported hepatotoxic botanicals in the US; stacking adds idiosyncratic liver-injury exposure.
edges.evidence: Population survey and DILI reviews; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Turmeric liver injury, like green tea injury, is hepatocellular and strongly linked to HLA-B*35:01; both are among the most reported hepatotoxic botanicals.
edges.evidence: DILIN case series and population survey; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Shared HLA-B*35:01-linked hepatocellular injury phenotype with turmeric/curcumin products; stacking hepatotoxic botanicals adds risk.
edges.evidence: DILIN case series and population survey; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury with jaundice, 8% transplant in DILIN; USP labeling advises not to use with a liver problem.
edges.evidence: DILIN series, USP review, LiverTox; moderate certainty

edges.mechanism: Carried by 72% of DILIN green tea liver-injury cases vs 11-12% of controls, suggesting immune-mediated idiosyncratic injury.
edges.evidence: Case-control genetic analysis within DILIN; NCCIH notes 5-15% carrier frequency; moderate certainty

edges.mechanism: Bolus doses on an empty stomach markedly increase EGCG bioavailability and are linked to hepatotoxicity; calorie restriction potentiated EGCG liver injury in mice; USP label says take with food.
edges.evidence: Human PK, toxicology reviews, animal data; moderate certainty

edges.mechanism: High-dose extract (843 mg EGCG/day) raised ALT 5.4 U/L and AST 3.8 U/L; 6.7% had ALT elevation; true hepatotoxic effect rather than assay artifact.
edges.evidence: Large RCT (MGTT); high certainty

edges.mechanism: Extracts may contain substantial undeclared caffeine; caffeine reference intake in pregnancy is 300 mg/day; no adequate safety data for high-dose extracts.
edges.evidence: Caffeine systematic review and NCCIH advice; low certainty
